_comment: Per-species attributes for Alberta Lepidoptera (schema v40, V2.12 'fly as a butterfly'). Parallels bee_attributes_master.json: one record per fauna row with taxon='lepidoptera', resolved at seed time by scientific_name. Fields are deliberately COARSE and honest (Design principle P9): flight_season is a plain month range for adult flight in central Alberta; nectar_flower_genera lists ADULT nectar-plant genera that occur in this app's plant database, and is null for species whose adults do not feed (giant silk moths and some sphinxes have vestigial mouthparts). overwintering_stage tells the gardener what to leave over winter (P8, P4). Larval host plants live in plant_fauna (relationship='larval_host'), not here.
_sources: Acorn, J. & Sheldon, I. (2006). Butterflies of Alberta.
Pohl, G.R., Anweiler, G.G., Schmidt, B.C. & Kondla, N.G. (2010). An annotated list of the Lepidoptera of Alberta, Canada. ZooKeys 38: 1-549.
Bird, C.D., Hilchie, G.J., Kondla, N.G., Pike, E.M. & Sperling, F.A.H. (1995). Alberta Butterflies.
Pohl, G.R., Landry, J.-F., Schmidt, B.C. et al. (2018). Annotated Checklist of the Moths and Butterflies of Canada and Alaska.

conservation_status: At Risk (COSEWIC Endangered); a rare breeding migrant in Alberta
notes: Late-summer nectar (goldenrods, asters, blazingstar) fuels the southward migration.

larval_host_note: Poplar, birch, willow, chokecherry and other broadleaf trees/shrubs.
notes: Alberta's common tiger swallowtail; puddles at damp soil, nectars at early shrubs.

larval_host_note: Willow, poplar and other riparian broadleaf trees.
notes: Reaches Alberta mainly in the southwest along river valleys.
Hilltopping males patrol ridges; larvae favour prairie sages.

larval_host_note: Willow, poplar, birch and elm foliage.
notes: Overwinters as an adult and is among the first butterflies on warm spring days; feeds mostly at tree sap and fallen fruit, only occasionally at flowers.
A nettle specialist as a caterpillar; adults overwinter and nectar readily at asters.
Like the mourning cloak, overwinters as an adult and prefers sap and rotting fruit to flowers.
In big flight years, clouds of painted ladies pour north into Alberta and swarm autumn asters.
A fast, territorial flier; nectars at asters but also takes tree sap and fallen fruit.
The white-banded admiral of poplar bluffs; feeds heavily at sap and honeydew, less at flowers.
A big orange fritillary; caterpillars need violets, adults love mid-summer thistles and coneflowers.
A montane/foothills fritillary; violets for the young, composite flowers for the adults.
A grassland satyr; grass-feeding caterpillars, occasional flower visits by adults.

larval_host_note: Flower buds of dogwood, cranberry and other shrubs.
notes: One of the earliest spring flutters of blue; adults work willow catkins and shrub blossom.

larval_host_note: Legume flowers and pods (milkvetch, vetch, lupine).
notes: A legume specialist tended by ants; nectars close to its host plants.
A tiny tailed-blue of legume patches and roadside vetch.
A late-summer skipper of dry grassland; adults nectar at autumn asters and goldenrod.

larval_host_note: Birch, poplar, willow, chokecherry, maple and other broadleaf trees.
notes: A giant silk moth: the adult has NO working mouthparts and does not feed — it lives only a week to mate. Support it with host trees and by leaving cocoons in the leaf litter over winter.

larval_host_note: Chokecherry, willow, birch, maple and apple.
notes: North America's largest moth. Adults do not feed; the papery brown cocoon overwinters on host-plant twigs — don't prune it off.

larval_host_note: Honeysuckle, snowberry and cranberry (Lonicera, Symphoricarpos, Viburnum).
notes: A day-flying 'hummingbird moth' that hovers at tubular flowers — often mistaken for a tiny hummingbird.
The bumblebee-mimic clearwing; day-active and a great pollinator of bee balm and phlox.

larval_host_note: Fireweed, evening-primrose, purslane and many herbs.
notes: A powerful hawkmoth that hovers at flowers from dusk into the night, and often by day too.
A heavy-bodied poplar sphinx; the adult's proboscis is reduced and it does not feed. Big green caterpillars ride the poplars.
The twin-spotted eyed sphinx flashes blue eyespots when disturbed; the adult does not feed.

larval_host_note: A wide range of low herbaceous plants.
notes: Its caterpillar is the familiar banded 'woolly bear' that overwinters frozen under leaf litter — leave the leaves.

larval_host_note: Poplar, willow, birch, alder and maple.
notes: A tiger moth whose spotted tussock caterpillar feeds on broadleaf trees; short-lived adults barely feed.
Our largest skipper; it visits pink, purple and red flowers but rarely yellow ones.
The common ringlet bobs low over meadow grass and sips at low forbs.
The clouded sulphur flies all season in yellow drifts over clover and legume fields.
A prairie blue tied to native legumes and their attendant ants.
A small orange crescent whose caterpillars and nectaring adults both depend on native asters.
